title: The daemon probes deployed environments on a durable schedule and raises one incident
description:
SPIDR child 1 of task-7683a432eb3f4e87b1eb0cbc6e3a55ff (architect-20a6d1eb, 2026-09-05). Dependency-free LEAF.

WHAT THIS ROW OWNS: the probe loop. For every environment with a deploy receipt, probe the health URL on a DURABLE schedule (default 60 s, per-environment setting), record `moe-health-probe/1` {environment, sha, status, latencyMs, at} in a BOUNDED ring (last 1440), derive UP / DEGRADED / DOWN, and raise exactly ONE Needs-you incident after three consecutive failures. No backups, no rollback, no UI.

MEASURED AT HEAD (branch moe/work-2026-09-04) by architect-20a6d1eb: `/health/read` reports the DAEMON's own health only (apps/daemon/src/http/health-read.ts, where KNOWN_PROVIDERS lives at :34); there is no probe of a deployed product anywhere. The gap is real.

THREE PROPERTIES THAT ARE EASY TO GET WRONG AND HARD TO NOTICE:
1. EXACTLY ONE INCIDENT. Three consecutive failures raise one card; continued failure must NOT raise a second, and recovery must CLOSE it. A loop that raises per-probe floods Needs-you at one card a minute and makes the queue useless precisely when the operator needs it.
2. THE RING IS BOUNDED at 1440. An unbounded probe log grows without limit in a durable store and is the kind of thing nobody notices until the store is huge.
3. SURVIVES A RESTART from durable records: no probe lost, and - the harder half - NO DOUBLE SCHEDULE. A restart that re-registers an already-scheduled probe doubles the rate silently, and the symptom is a store filling twice as fast rather than an error.

COORDINATION, not a dependency: the deploy receipt this reads belongs to task-04b3ce7e349743c2a156d32ee5550ba5 under a SIBLING parent (containerized deployment), which the parent rail forbids depending on. If it has not landed, build against the receipt shape recorded there and say so in the record - do not invent a different one, because child 2's rollback resolves through the same receipts.
definitionOfDone: A probe loop test with a FAKE target drives UP -> DOWN: three consecutive failures raise EXACTLY ONE incident card, continued failure raises NO second card, and recovery CLOSES it. Assert the card count across many failing probes - a per-probe raise floods the queue at one card a minute exactly when the operator needs it usable.

The ring is BOUNDED at 1440: after more than 1440 probes the oldest are gone and the newest are present, asserted by count and by content. An unbounded durable probe log is invisible until the store is large.

PROBES SURVIVE A DAEMON RESTART from durable records: no probe is lost, and NO DOUBLE SCHEDULE - assert the probe RATE after a restart equals the rate before. A silently doubled schedule shows up as a store filling twice as fast, never as an error.

`moe-health-probe/1` records {environment, sha, status, latencyMs, at} and the derived UP / DEGRADED / DOWN state is a function of the ring, not a stored flag - assert the state changes when the ring does, so the two cannot disagree.

The per-environment interval setting is honoured (default 60 s) and PROBE_URL_MISSING refuses with code + layer for an environment with a deploy receipt but no health URL - an environment that cannot be probed says so rather than reporting UP.
Gates quoted with their `Test Files N passed` count lines: `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test`, `pnpm typecheck`.
taskRails: EXACTLY ONE INCIDENT PER OUTAGE. A per-probe raise makes Needs-you unusable at the moment it matters most.
THE RING IS BOUNDED. A durable log with no ceiling is a slow leak nobody sees.
NO DOUBLE SCHEDULE ON RESTART. Assert the rate, not just that probing resumed.
AN UNPROBEABLE ENVIRONMENT IS NEVER 'UP'. Absence of a health URL is a refusal, not a green state.
NO BACKUPS, NO ROLLBACK, NO UI: those are children 2 and 3. The deploy receipt comes from a SIBLING parent's row (task-04b3ce7e) - build against its recorded shape, do not invent a second one.

implementationPlan.description:
CONFIRM THE TWO CHILDREN DELIVERED. This row is a SPIDR shell: it was split because it needed the daemon's FIRST recurring loop plus a probe, a bounded ring, a derived state and an incident — five pieces over twelve-plus files. Both children are named in this row's dependsOn:
  - grandchild A task-e651725c92434127a7b8d72f0ac5246b — the durable recurring schedule (DoD 3, and the interval half of DoD 5)
  - grandchild B task-cc05c47362dc41b0b2b416a70ad45b42 — the probe, the bounded ring, the derived state, the durable incident (DoD 1, 2, 4, and the PROBE_URL_MISSING half of DoD 5)

Write NO production code here. A shortfall routes back to the child that owns it via a comment and an amendment.

Re-measure the two facts that drove the split, at the DELIVERED tree:
  (a) `grep -rn 'setInterval' apps/daemon/src --include=*.ts | grep -v '\.test\.'` — at plan time this returned ZERO, which is why grandchild A exists at all. It should now show A's scheduler and NOTHING ELSE: a second, independently-armed timer somewhere in the probe code would mean B armed its own rather than consuming A's registration seam, and that is the double-schedule hazard wearing a different coat.
  (b) `grep -rn 'NEEDS_YOU_KINDS' apps/control-room/src --include=*.ts` — the roster must STILL be the closed four (PLAN_APPROVAL, ESCALATION, GATE_1, READY_TO_CLOSE). If a fifth kind appeared, a child made the UI change this row's rail 5 forbids; say so and route it back rather than accepting it.

Read each child's verification, completionSummary and reviewSummary from get_context.epicSiblings rather than re-deriving their work.

CONFIRM THE THREE PROPERTIES THE PARENT NAMED AS EASY TO GET WRONG AND HARD TO NOTICE. Each has a specific way of passing while being broken, so check the ASSERTION SHAPE, not just that an arm exists.

(a) EXACTLY ONE INCIDENT (DoD 1). Confirm B's arm counts incidents across MANY failing probes and a recovery — three failures open one, a further run of failures opens NO second, recovery closes it. An arm that checks only "an incident exists after three failures" passes for a loop that opens one per probe, which floods the operator's queue at one item a minute exactly when it must stay usable.

(b) THE RING IS BOUNDED (DoD 2). Confirm the arm asserts by COUNT AND BY CONTENT after more than 1440 probes. A count-only assertion passes for a ring that evicts the NEWEST instead of the oldest — same size, wrong contents, and the probe history is silently useless.

(c) NO DOUBLE SCHEDULE (DoD 3). Confirm A's arm compares the post-restart execution RATE to the pre-restart rate over the same window. "Probing resumed" is the assertion that lets a doubled schedule ship, and its only symptom is a durable store filling twice as fast — never an error.

Then confirm DoD 4's derivation: the UP/DEGRADED/DOWN state follows a MUTATED ring with no write. If the state is stored anywhere, the ring and the flag are two sources of truth that can disagree about the same history.

And DoD 5's refusal: an environment with a deploy receipt but no health URL is NOT reported UP — assert the state, not merely that a refusal was returned. An unprobeable environment reporting green is the worst output this feature can produce.

GATES AND CLOSE, AND STATE THE TWO SCOPE FACTS PLAINLY.

GATES, each STANDALONE and FOREGROUND — no pipe, no `;` chain, no `&&` (a piped run reports tail's exit code; a chain reports only the last command's):
  1. `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test`
  2. `pnpm typecheck`
READ THE OUTPUT, NOT THE EXIT CODE: a missed `--filter` exits 0, and "No test files found" / "0 passed" are also exit 0. The discriminator is `Test Files N passed` with N nonzero — quote it for both. A bare `pnpm test` covers no `apps/**` and is not evidence here. Name `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test` as this row's complete_task verification command.

The daemon suite is slow (~22 min) and flaky on this branch (two back-to-back baselines gave `17 failed | 416 passed` then `10 failed | 423 passed`, dominated by 30000ms timeouts), so attribute red by PATH per global rail 3. This row owns NO production paths, so any red belongs to a child or a peer — report it verbatim with exact failing lines and paths, disclosed and never fabricated green.

THE COMPLETION RECORD MUST STATE BOTH OF THESE, because a grader reading the parent's DoD 1 will otherwise think a criterion is unmet:
  - DoD 1 SHIPPED AS A DURABLE INCIDENT, NOT A NEEDS-YOU CARD. Needs-you is a control-room model over a CLOSED four-kind roster (needs-you-model.ts:28) whose items are "derived only from things the daemon already states" and which all route to a goal. A deployment outage is a fifth kind that routes to an environment, so the card is a UI change and rail 5 forbids it here. "Exactly one incident" is delivered and asserted as a property of the durable record — one open per outage, closed on recovery — and a later UI row derives the card from it.
  - THE DEPLOY RECEIPT WAS UNLANDED at plan time (`grep -rn 'deploy-receipt|moe-deploy-receipt|DeployReceipt' apps packages --include=*.ts` returned ZERO). It belongs to task-04b3ce7e under a SIBLING parent, which the parent rail forbids depending on. Record which shape B actually built against and whether that row has since landed — the sibling rollback work resolves through the same receipts, so a divergence here is a real defect rather than a cosmetic one.

planningNotes.approachesConsidered:
PLANNING IT WHOLE — rejected on measurement: a new scheduler module and bridge and test, a probe module, a bounded-ring record store, a derived-state function and an incident module, plus daemon-main wiring, is comfortably past ten distinct files, and the daemon has no scheduler to build on.

WHERE THE SEAM WENT: INFRASTRUCTURE vs FEATURE. Grandchild A is the durable recurring schedule — generic, reusable, and the piece carrying the subtle double-schedule hazard. Grandchild B is the probe, the ring, the derived state and the incident, which are one coherent feature over ~3 modules and share the same durable records. That is a contract boundary: B consumes A's registration seam, so the dependency is real build order rather than paperwork.

THREE CHILDREN (splitting the incident from the probe) — rejected. The incident's "exactly one" property is a function of the probe ring's failure run, so separating them would put the property and its input in different rows and force one to assert against the other's unlanded surface. They belong together.

MAKING THE INCIDENT A NEEDS-YOU KIND HERE — rejected on two independent grounds: the parent's rail 5 forbids UI work, and the Needs-you model is derivation-based and goal-routed, so a pushed, environment-routed fifth kind would violate its stated design rather than extend it. The durable record is the honest deliverable at this layer.

GIVING GRANDCHILD A HEALTH-PROBE VOCABULARY — rejected: it is the daemon's first scheduled work and B is its first consumer, not its owner. A generic scheduler keeps the next consumer from needing a second one.
planningNotes.codebaseInsights:
MEASURED 2026-09-05 by architect-aa54e231 on branch moe/work-2026-09-04. This row was SPLIT rather than planned: it needed five separable pieces and projected past both the file and step caps.

THE DAEMON HAS NO RECURRING LOOP AT ALL. `grep -rn 'setInterval' apps/daemon/src --include=*.ts` excluding tests returns ZERO, and daemon-main.ts has no periodic tick — everything today is request-driven or spawn-driven. So "probe on a durable schedule" is not adding a timer to an existing scheduler; it is the daemon's FIRST scheduled work. That is a subsystem in its own right and it is precisely where the parent's DoD 3 double-schedule hazard comes from, so it became grandchild A as the dependency-free leaf.

THE PARENT'S DoD 1 CANNOT BE MET AS WORDED WITHOUT BREAKING ITS OWN RAIL 5. Needs-you is a CONTROL-ROOM model, not a server-side table. `apps/control-room/src/v2/approvals/needs-you-model.ts:28` declares a CLOSED roster — NEEDS_YOU_KINDS = ["PLAN_APPROVAL", "ESCALATION", "GATE_1", "READY_TO_CLOSE"] — and its docblock states the governing principle: every item is "derived only from things the daemon already states", each rests on a daemon OFFER or read (the file is explicit that nothing infers reviewability from a lifecycle word), and "Every item routes to the goal". A deployment outage is a FIFTH kind that routes to an ENVIRONMENT, not a goal. Adding it is a control-room change, and the parent's own rail 5 says NO UI (children 2 and 3 own it). The seam is therefore: grandchild B writes the DURABLE INCIDENT with its open/closed lifecycle — where "exactly one" is fully assertable — and a later UI row derives the card. Both children are told to state this in their records so the criterion is not read as unmet.

THE DEPLOY RECEIPT IS UNLANDED. `grep -rn 'deploy-receipt|moe-deploy-receipt|DeployReceipt' apps packages --include=*.ts` returns ZERO. It belongs to task-04b3ce7e under a SIBLING parent, and the parent rail forbids a dependsOn on it, so grandchild B builds against the shape recorded on that row and says so — the sibling rollback work resolves through the same receipts, which is why inventing a second shape would be a real defect.

THE LIFECYCLE DISCIPLINE TO COPY, for grandchild A: verifier-process-runner.ts takes `spawn`, `timeoutMs`, `killGraceMs` and `killProcessGroup` as injectable options (:45-56) and has ONE idempotent `cleanup()` called on every exit path (:107-118). A scheduler needs exactly that shape, plus an injected clock — this host has a measured spawn-latency cliff that reds timing-sensitive tests for unrelated reasons, so no arm may wait on wall-clock time.
planningNotes.risks:
1. B ARMING ITS OWN TIMER. If grandchild B calls setInterval directly instead of consuming A's registration seam, the row ships two schedulers and the double-schedule hazard returns by a different route. Step 1 greps for exactly that: A's scheduler should be the ONLY setInterval in production code.

2. THE INCIDENT ARM THAT PASSES FOR A FLOOD. "An incident exists after three failures" is satisfied by a loop that opens one per probe. Only counting across a long failing run and a recovery distinguishes them, and the failure mode — one queue item a minute — degrades the operator's queue precisely when it is needed.

3. THE RING THAT EVICTS THE WRONG END. A count-only bound assertion passes for a ring that drops the newest and keeps 1440 stale entries. Same size, useless contents. DoD 2 requires count AND content.

4. "PROBING RESUMED" AS THE RESTART ASSERTION. It passes for a doubled schedule, whose only symptom is a store filling twice as fast. Only a RATE comparison over the same window catches it.

5. A STORED STATE FLAG. If UP/DEGRADED/DOWN is written rather than derived, the flag and the ring become two sources of truth about one history and will eventually disagree. DoD 4 requires the state to follow a mutated ring with no write.

6. AN UNPROBEABLE ENVIRONMENT REPORTING UP. The worst output this feature can produce, and the natural implementation (no probe result, so no failure, so healthy) produces it. The refusal must make the state not-UP, and the arm must assert the STATE rather than the refusal.

7. TIMING-SENSITIVE ARMS. This host has a measured spawn-latency cliff (~10 s stalls) that reds timing tests for unrelated reasons; a scheduler tested on a real clock would be flaky and slow. A's rails require an injected clock and timer throughout.

8. A LEAKED INTERVAL. Timers keep node alive: a schedule with no shutdown path makes the daemon unkillable and contaminates every neighbouring test.
